master_output.idea:
Let me start from what I trust rather than from what the code already does. My anchor: the limiting factor is not compute or data here — it's the model's ability to generalize from its training distribution to the test distribution. So the bottleneck lives inside the model itself, not outside of it. That's where I should look first.

Now let me inspect the code with that in mind. train.py appears to be a standard supervised classifier setup: load data, define a model (looks like a CNN), train it end-to-end with cross-entropy loss, evaluate on validation. This is exactly the kind of architecture that tends to overfit to spurious correlations in the training data, because it learns one global representation that must work everywhere. And the symptom I expect is that the model will perform well on easy, clean, in-distribution examples but poorly on any test examples that deviate slightly from the training distribution — precisely the kind of failure I'm trying to prevent.

So the leap: don't fix this by throwing more data or more epochs at it. Fix it by changing the objective the model is optimizing — and specifically by adding an auxiliary self-supervised task that forces the model to learn structure from the data itself, rather than relying solely on the labels. A good candidate is rotation prediction: take each image, rotate it by 0°, 90°, 180°, or 270° at random, and train the network to predict which rotation was applied. Why rotation? Because it's a cheap, natural augmentation that exposes the model to variations in the input while keeping the object identity intact — so the model has to learn to recognize the object regardless of its orientation, which is a form of invariance that transfers well across the test distribution.

But the real crux is not just adding rotation. It's how you combine it with the main classification objective. If I naively concatenate the rotation-prediction logits with the class-prediction logits into one big loss, the model will optimize a weighted average of the two objectives, and the larger, cleaner classification signal will dominate the weaker, noisier rotation signal, rendering the whole exercise ineffective. Instead, I want to keep the rotation branch separate and give it its own head, so it can be optimized independently. Then I'll use the features from the shared backbone as a regularizer for the classification branch via a regularization term in the loss — e.g., a consistency term that penalizes large differences between the backbone features before and after the rotation. This way the rotation task pulls the backbone toward a representation that's invariant to orientation, while the classification task still gets to focus on its own decision boundary.

Why does this cut against the room? Most people would reflexively reach for data augmentation or more training epochs first; the instinct to change the objective itself is less common. And even among those who add auxiliary tasks, few think through the combination mechanism carefully enough to avoid the dominant-signal problem.

Core idea: Add a rotation-prediction self-supervised auxiliary task with its own head, and regularize the main classification branch using backbone features' consistency across rotations.

Non-trivial crux: The rotation branch must have its own head and be combined via feature-consistency regularization, not via a naive concatenated-loss approach, to ensure the weaker rotation signal isn't dominated by the stronger classification signal.
